title: Seattle Sounders Schedule Today: CF Montreal Game Details
summary: Find out when Seattle Sounders vs. CF Montreal starts, how to watch live, and key facts about the 2026 MLS season.
intro: The Seattle Sounders are on the schedule for Sunday, October 18, 2026, when they host CF Montreal. The match kicks off at 10:30 p.m. local time and will be streamed live through Sounder at Heart. Coach Brian Schmetzer leads the team in its 18th MLS season, and the game counts toward the regular‑season standings. Below you’ll find everything you need to know about today’s fixture, where to watch, and quick reference facts for fans.
bullets: Match: Seattle Sounders vs. CF Montreal

sections.heading: When does the Seattle Sounders vs. CF Montreal game start today?
sections.text: The Seattle Sounders take the field against CF Montreal at 10:30 p.m. on Sunday, October 18, 2026. The late kickoff gives fans a chance to catch the action after work or dinner. Because the game is part of the MLS regular season, the result will affect both teams’ standings as they push toward the playoffs. Make sure your calendar reflects the correct time zone for Seattle (Pacific Daylight Time) to avoid missing the first whistle.

sections.heading: Where can I watch the Seattle Sounders vs. CF Montreal match live?
sections.text: Live coverage will be available through the Sounder at Heart streaming platform on October 18. The service provides a high‑definition feed of the match, complete with commentary and post‑game analysis. Additionally, the Universidad de Córdoba (UCO) site lists the game as a live‑stream option for both the 17th and 18th of October, giving fans an alternative source if you encounter any technical issues with Sounder at Heart. sections.heading: Is the Seattle Sounders game today part of the MLS regular season schedule?
sections.text: Yes. The October 18 fixture is an official MLS regular‑season contest. Both Seattle Sounders FC and CF Montreal are competing for points that determine playoff eligibility and seeding. The match follows the league’s standard points system—three points for a win, one for a draw, and none for a loss. As the season approaches its final stretch, each result becomes increasingly important for teams fighting for a postseason berth.

sections.heading: Who is the head coach of the Seattle Sounders for the 2026 season?
sections.text:
Brian Schmetzer continues as the head coach of Seattle Sounders FC for the 2026 season, marking his seventh full year at the helm of the club.  Schmetzer, a Seattle native and former Sounders player, took over the senior team in 2016 after serving as an assistant and leading the club’s academy.  His deep familiarity with the roster—built around home‑grown talent such as Jordan Morris, Cristian Roldan and the emerging midfield duo of Danny Leyva and Nate Clark—has allowed him to maintain a consistent tactical identity while integrating new signings.  Under his guidance, the Sounders have already logged their 18th MLS campaign, a milestone that underscores the longevity of his tenure in a league where turnover is common.

Schmetzer’s experience is especially valuable as the club prepares for a pivotal matchup against CF Montreal on Sunday, 18 October 2026. The October 18 game against CF Montreal adds to this total, bringing the club closer to the end of the regular season and the start of the playoff picture.

title: Living in Frisco TX: What New Residents Need to Know
summary: Discover population, location, climate, shopping, and economic development facts for living in Frisco, TX.
intro: Frisco, Texas, sits in Collin and Denton counties about 25 miles from both Dallas Love Field and DFW International Airport. With a 2020 census population of 200,509, it’s a fast‑growing suburb of the Dallas‑Fort Worth metroplex offering ample retail, a mild climate, and a unique funding model for economic development.
bullets: Major malls include Stonebriar Centre and IKEA
Economic development funded by local sales tax

sections.heading: Population and Growth Trends
sections.text: Frisco’s 2020 census count stood at 200,509 residents, making it one of the largest cities in the Dallas‑Fort Worth area. The city earned the title of fastest‑growing U.S. city in 2017 and maintained rapid expansion from 2000 to 2009. This growth is reflected in the larger McKinney‑Frisco urban area, which reached 504,803 people in 2020, ranking 83rd nationwide. The surge in residents has spurred new housing, schools, and businesses, creating a dynamic environment for newcomers.

sections.heading: Location and Transportation
sections.text: Frisco lies roughly 25 miles (40 km) north of both Dallas Love Field and Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport, providing easy access for travelers and commuters. The city’s main north‑south artery, Preston Road, is lined with retail and dining options and connects to major highways. While Frisco does not participate in Dallas Area Rapid Transit, it funds its Economic Development Corporation through a fractional percent of local sales tax, a model that differs from many neighboring DFW municipalities.

sections.heading: Climate and Weather Patterns
sections.text: Frisco experiences a humid subtropical climate, averaging 39 inches (990 mm) of precipitation annually. Residents enjoy about 230 sunny days each year, with July highs reaching 96 °F (36 °C) and January lows dropping to 33 °F (1 °C). The city sits in Tornado Alley; the most recent confirmed tornado was an EF‑0 in 2024 near the UNT Frisco Campus. Seasonal variations are moderate, making outdoor activities feasible for most of the year.

sections.heading: Retail and Shopping Destinations
sections.text:
Shopping in Frisco is anchored by the 165‑store Stonebriar Centre, a regional mall that draws visitors from across the Dallas–Fort Worth metroplex. Beyond the usual fashion and electronics retailers, the mall houses a cinema complex, a full‑service spa, and a seasonal indoor farmers market, giving residents a one‑stop destination for both everyday needs and special occasions. Just a short drive east, IKEA’s 310,000‑square‑foot showroom offers everything from Scandinavian‑style furniture to a sprawling kitchen‑display area, making home‑renovation projects feel less like a chore and more like an outing.

The retail corridor along Preston Road amplifies the city’s shopping appeal. This north–south artery is lined with boutique clothing shops, specialty food stores, and an eclectic mix of restaurants ranging from upscale steakhouses to casual taco joints. Because Frisco sits only about 25 miles from both Dallas Love Field and DFW International Airport, the area attracts out‑of‑town shoppers who appreciate the convenience of high‑quality retail without the traffic of downtown Dallas.

In addition to these flagship venues, Frisco’s Economic Development Corporation reinvests a fraction of local sales tax into further retail growth, encouraging new concepts such as pop‑up markets and artisan fairs. The result is a dynamic shopping landscape that reflects the city’s rapid growth—its population surged to 200,509 in the 2020 census—and its commitment to providing residents with diverse, convenient, and locally supported retail experiences—all without leaving the 62‑square‑mile city limits.

sections.heading: Economic Development Funding Model
sections.text:
Unlike many DFW municipalities that lean on regional transit taxes, Frisco finances its Economic Development Corporation (EDC) with a fractional percent of the city’s own sales tax. Each dollar spent at a Frisco retailer contributes a small, earmarked portion—currently 0.1 % of the local sales‑tax base—to a dedicated fund that the city controls directly. Because the money never passes through the Dallas Area Rapid Transit system, the EDC can allocate resources on a quarterly basis to projects that match Frisco’s unique growth trajectory.

The model has paid dividends since the city’s population surged to 200,509 in the 2020 census and the McKinney‑Frisco urban area topped half a million residents. With rapid expansion comes a need for targeted infrastructure: the sales‑tax pool has financed upgrades to Preston Road, added bike lanes near the Stonebriar Centre, and supported the construction of a new transit hub near The Star, home of the Dallas Cowboys headquarters. It also backs incentives that attract national retailers—such as the 310,000‑square‑foot IKEA and the 165‑store Stonebriar Centre—by offering site‑improvement grants and streamlined permitting.

Because the funding is locally sourced, Frisco can match its economic goals with community priorities, from preserving green space (the city has been a Tree City USA since 2003) to funding public‑art installations in new mixed‑use districts. This tailored approach ensures that as the city expands across its 62.4 square‑mile footprint, growth remains purposeful, locally driven, and responsive to the needs of new residents.

sections.heading: Recreation and Community Amenities
sections.text: Since 2003, Frisco has held the Tree City USA designation, reflecting a commitment to green space and urban forestry. The city’s 62.4 square miles include parks, trails, and the notable Star, home to the Dallas Cowboys headquarters. These amenities, combined with a low water footprint—only 0.92% of the city’s area—offer residents ample opportunities for outdoor recreation and community events.

sections.heading: Living Costs and Housing Overview
sections.text: While specific price data is not provided, Frisco’s rapid growth and extensive retail and corporate presence suggest a competitive housing market. The city’s proximity to major airports and highways, coupled with its robust economic development funding, supports a range of housing options from new subdivisions to established neighborhoods. Prospective residents should consider the city’s amenities, climate, and transportation links when budgeting for a move.

faq.a: Frisco lies about 25 miles (40 km) north of both Dallas Love Field and Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport, offering convenient access for travelers.

faq.a: Key retail centers include Stonebriar Centre, a 165‑store regional mall, and a 310,000‑square‑foot IKEA store, both drawing shoppers from across the region.

faq.a: Frisco has a humid subtropical climate with 39 inches of annual precipitation, about 230 sunny days, July highs near 96 °F and January lows around 33 °F.

faq.a: Frisco uses a fractional percent of local sales tax to fund its Economic Development Corporation, unlike many neighboring cities that rely on regional transit taxes.

conclusion: Living in Frisco, TX offers a blend of rapid growth, convenient airport access, abundant shopping, and a sunny climate. Understanding the city’s population size, funding model, and amenities helps newcomers make informed decisions about settling in this thriving Dallas‑Fort Worth suburb.

title: When Is Columbus Marathon 2026? Dates, Route & Details
summary: Find the exact dates, start/finish location, road closures and runner count for the 2026 Columbus Marathon.
intro: The 2026 Columbus Marathon is set for the weekend of October 16-18, 2026. The race kicks off Saturday, October 16, and finishes on Tuesday, October 18 at North Bank Park. Expect about 15,000 runners, new course changes, and citywide road closures on all three days. This guide gives you the essential facts you need to plan your weekend.
bullets: Start: Saturday, Oct 16; Finish: Tue, Oct 18 at North Bank Park

sections.heading: Exact Dates of the 2026 Columbus Marathon
sections.text: The Columbus Marathon weekend runs from Saturday, October 16 to Tuesday, October 18, 2026. The official kickoff is on Saturday, with the full marathon concluding on Tuesday at North Bank Park. As of October 2026, these dates are confirmed by local broadcasters 10TV and WSYX. Mark your calendar early, especially if you plan to watch the finish or volunteer, because the event spans three days of activity across the city.

sections.heading: Start and Finish Locations for 2026
sections.text: Runners will line up at the start line on Saturday, October 16, with the course winding through downtown Columbus before looping back to finish at North Bank Park on Tuesday, October 18. North Bank Park, located along the Scioto River, serves as the final destination for the marathon, half‑marathon and other race divisions. The start location and finish line are both situated near major transit hubs, making it easy for spectators and participants to access public transportation.

sections.heading: Road Closures During the Marathon Weekend
sections.text: City officials have announced road closures for October 16, 17 and 18, 2026. Major arteries in downtown Columbus, including portions of High Street and the Scioto Mile, will be closed to vehicle traffic while the race proceeds. Detour routes are posted on the Columbus Department of Transportation website, and signage will be in place the day before each closure. Residents and commuters should plan alternate routes or use public transit to avoid delays.

sections.heading: Runner Participation Numbers
sections.text:
The 2026 Columbus Marathon is projected to draw approximately 15,000 runners, a figure confirmed by WSYX and echoed across local media outlets. This sizable field is a blend of elite competitors, seasoned club athletes, and a wave of first‑time marathoners eager to experience the city’s newly unveiled course. Over the past decade, participant numbers have risen steadily, positioning the Columbus Marathon as one of the Midwest’s most sought‑after road races and a key fixture on the national marathon calendar.

The influx of runners translates into a bustling race‑week experience. An expanded marathon expo will open at the Ohio Expo Center on Friday, October 17, offering vendors, gear demos, and health‑screening stations to accommodate the larger crowd. Meanwhile, a volunteer network of more than 2,000 locals—students, retirees, and community groups—will staff water stations, course marshals, and finish‑line services across the three‑day road‑closure window (October 16‑18). 

Finisher celebrations are set for Tuesday, October 18, at North Bank Park, where a post‑race festival will feature live music, food trucks, and a medal ceremony for all 15,000 participants. The scale of the event also means increased logistical coordination with the city: traffic detours, public‑transport adjustments, and enhanced safety patrols will be in place throughout downtown Columbus to ensure a smooth experience for runners and spectators alike.

sections.heading: New Course for the 2026 Marathon
sections.text: The Columbus Dispatch reported that the 2026 marathon will follow a newly designed route. While the start and finish remain familiar, the middle sections have been adjusted to showcase different neighborhoods and improve runner flow. Organizers say the changes were made after extensive community feedback and aim to reduce congestion on popular streets. Runners can expect fresh scenery, new elevation points, and updated aid stations along the revised course.

faq.a: The marathon weekend runs from Saturday, October 16 to Tuesday, October 18, 2026, with the race beginning on the 16th and finishing at North Bank Park on the 18th.

faq.q: Where does the 2026 Columbus Marathon start and finish?
faq.a: The race starts on Saturday, October 16, in downtown Columbus and concludes on Tuesday, October 18 at North Bank Park along the Scioto River.

faq.q: What road closures will affect the city during the 2026 marathon?
faq.a: Road closures are planned for October 16, 17 and 18, affecting downtown streets such as High Street and sections of the Scioto Mile, with detour signage posted in advance.

faq.a: Organizers anticipate about 15,000 runners across all race divisions, based on reports from WSYX.

Plan for road closures, use public transit, and enjoy the city’s festive atmosphere as the marathon rolls through. With clear dates and routes, you can schedule travel, cheering spots, or volunteer shifts without surprise.
